Home.title: AI Consumer Rights
Home.lead: Plain-language help when AI makes decisions about you.

Guide.metaDescription: Plain-language help with chatbots, recommendations, and automated screening, with US and EU rules side by side and three calm steps to take.
Guide.title: AI you can question
Guide.lead: AI now helps make many everyday decisions. You can ask how it works, ask for a person, and talk it through. This page shows you how, with the rules in the US and the EU side by side.

touchpoints.heading: Spot the AI in your day
touchpoints.lead: Three kinds of AI touch most people's lives. Each one is easier to question once you know its name.

chatbots.what: answer questions in a chat window or on the phone. They are often fast and helpful. They can also state something false with confidence.
chatbots.ask: Am I talking to AI? Where can I check this answer?
chatbots.rule1: Since 2 August 2026, a chatbot must tell you it is AI, unless that is obvious.
chatbots.rule2: No federal law requires this. Some states do, and the rules differ by state.

recommendations.what: pick what you see next: videos, products, news, and ads. They learn from what you click, watch, and buy.
recommendations.ask: Why am I seeing this? Can I turn off personal suggestions?
recommendations.rule1: UNESCO's global standard on AI ethics says AI systems do not replace human responsibility, and it asks for transparency.
recommendations.rule2: The US Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights asks for plain notice and explanation. Neither one is binding law.

screening.what: sorts applications for loans, jobs, apartments, and insurance. Software may score your file before a person sees it.
screening.ask: Did software help decide? What were the main reasons?
screening.rule1: A lender that turns you down must give the specific main reasons.
screening.rule2: When a machine alone makes a serious decision about you, you can ask for a person to review it.

compare.heading: Compare the rules in the US, the EU, and other countries
compare.lead: They all want AI that people can trust. They take different routes. The US mostly applies existing laws, one sector and one state at a time. The EU passed one broad AI law and pairs it with its privacy law. Pick a country to compare it with both.
compare.caption: Rules compared: US, EU, and {country}, as of {date}

br.name: Brazil
br.intro: Brazil's data protection law, the LGPD, gives people a right to ask for a review of automated decisions.

it.name: Italy
it.intro: Italy follows EU rules and adds its own national AI law.

fr.name: France
fr.intro: France follows EU rules. Its own laws add rights when a public body uses an algorithm.

de.name: Germany
de.intro: Germany follows EU rules. It has a national AI supervisor, and new credit-score rights start on 20 November 2026.

in.name: India
in.intro: India has no AI-specific law. Its data protection law's main rights start in May 2027, and online platforms must label realistic AI-made content.

told.question: Will I be told it is AI?
told.us: No federal rule. Some states require it.
told.eu: Yes, since 2 August 2026, unless it is obvious.
told.br: Not yet required by a national AI law. Bill PL 2338/2023, passed by the Senate in December 2024, would require it. It is still a bill.
told.it: EU rules apply. Italy's AI law adds more: professionals must tell clients, in clear and simple words, which AI systems they use. Employers must inform workers.
told.fr: EU rules apply. France adds two rules. A public body must tell you when it used an algorithm to decide about you. Paid influencers must label AI-made images of a face or body as "Images virtuelles".
told.de: EU rules apply. Germany adds a rule for prices: online sellers must tell you if a price was personalized by an automated decision. From 20 November 2026, lenders must also tell you if a loan offer was personalized this way.
told.in: Partly. Since 20 February 2026, online platforms must clearly label realistic AI-made or AI-changed pictures, video, and sound. The sources checked show no general rule that you must be told when you deal with an AI system, such as a chatbot.

reasons.question: Can I get the reasons for a decision?
reasons.us: Yes for credit: the specific main reasons.
reasons.eu: You can ask for meaningful information about how an automated decision was made.
reasons.br: You can ask for clear information on the criteria and procedures used, within trade-secret limits. A request for your data gets a complete answer within 15 days.
reasons.it: GDPR rights apply, as across the EU. In health care, you have the right to be told when AI is used.
reasons.fr: GDPR rights apply, as across the EU. If a public body used an algorithm to decide about you, you can ask how: what data it used, where the data came from, and how much the algorithm counted.
reasons.de: GDPR rights apply, as across the EU. From 20 November 2026, whoever makes a credit score must tell you, on request and in plain words, which of your data and factors shaped it most.
reasons.in: No specific right to reasons. From May 2027, you can ask a company for a summary of your personal data and how it is used, and it must answer within 90 days. The law gives no right to an explanation of an automated decision.

review.question: Can a person review it?
review.us: No general federal right. The 2022 Blueprint recommends it, but it is not law.
review.eu: Yes, when a machine alone made a decision with a legal or similarly serious effect.
review.br: Yes, for decisions made solely by automated processing. The law no longer says a person must do the review.
review.it: GDPR Article 22 applies. Italy's law adds: in health care the decision always stays with the doctor, and in public administration the person stays solely responsible.
review.fr: Yes, under EU rules (GDPR). France adds more: a machine alone can never decide your appeal to a public body, and a court can't judge your behavior based only on automated profiling.
review.de: Yes, under EU rules. The EU Court of Justice (case C-634/21) said a credit score can count as an automated decision when a lender relies on it heavily. From 20 November 2026, you can challenge a score-based decision and have a person decide.
review.in: No right to a human review of an automated decision. From May 2027, you can ask for wrong data to be corrected, and data used to make a decision about you must be complete and accurate.

enforce.question: Who checks the rules?
enforce.us: The FTC says existing law has no AI exemption. The CFPB covers credit.
enforce.eu: National authorities in each EU country.
enforce.br: The national data protection authority (ANPD). It can audit a system for discrimination when trade secrets limit what you are told.
enforce.it: The data protection authority (Garante) keeps its powers to inspect, block, and fine. The AI law names two national AI authorities: AgID and ACN.
enforce.fr: The data protection authority (CNIL) checks data rules, and the consumer agency (DGCCRF) checks consumer rules. France has not yet named its EU AI Act authorities in law.
enforce.de: The Bundesnetzagentur checks the EU AI Act rules and takes AI complaints for the whole country. The financial supervisor (BaFin) covers AI in finance. Federal and state data protection authorities cover personal data.
enforce.in: The Data Protection Board of India. The law set it up in November 2025, but its power to hear complaints and fine starts in May 2027. In May 2026 the government invited applications for its members. Appeals about platform content go to the Grievance Appellate Committee.

changing.question: What is changing?
changing.us: A December 2025 executive order calls for one national approach and a review of state AI laws.
changing.eu: Rules for high-risk AI, like hiring and credit, now start on 2 December 2027.
changing.br: Bill PL 2338/2023 would add a risk-based AI law with rights to an explanation, to contest decisions, and to human review. As of 23 September 2026, it waits for a report in a special committee of the Chamber of Deputies.
changing.it: Law No. 132/2025, Italy's national AI law, has been in force since 10 October 2025. It works alongside the EU AI Act. Children under 14 need a parent's consent to use AI.
changing.fr: A bill passed by the Senate on 18 February 2026 would make the CNIL France's main AI authority and let it handle AI complaints. As of 27 September 2026, it waits for a vote in the National Assembly.
changing.de: Germany's AI supervision law (KI-MIG) has been in force since 29 July 2026. From 20 November 2026, credit scores may not use your address, age, gender, name, social media, bank account payments, or sensitive data such as health, and may not be made about children.
changing.in: The main data rights start in May 2027. A draft rule, open for comment until May 2026, would keep AI labels visible for the whole length of a video. The government's AI guidelines (November 2025) are not binding and say no separate AI law is needed yet.

steps.heading: Take three calm steps when a decision seems wrong
steps.lead: Start small and stay specific. Most problems get fixed at step one. Use the arrow keys or tap a step to move between them.
steps.helpLink: Need a letter to send? <help>Pick what happened to you</help>.

everyone.heading: See every side of the table
everyone.lead: Most people in this story are trying to do right by others. A question asked in good faith usually gets a better answer.
everyone.peopleText: want fair answers and a simple way to ask questions.
everyone.educatorsText: are teaching new skills quickly, often with few resources.
everyone.regulatorsText: weigh safety against new ideas, and good rules take time to write.
everyone.buildersText: often want feedback. A clear, specific question helps them fix real problems.
everyone.research1: Experts and the public often see AI differently. Stanford's AI Index found a 50-point gap between them on how AI will affect jobs.
everyone.research2: In a Pew survey of 5,119 US adults, most said AI is moving too fast.
everyone.research3: Honest questions help close gaps like these.
everyone.voiceLink: Vote on shared ideas in the forum

explorer.tablistLabel: Three steps when a decision seems wrong
explorer.noWhereElse: No, where else can I turn?
explorer.announceSettled: Settled. Keep a copy of your messages.
explorer.resolvedBody: Save a copy of your messages and the reply. If the same issue comes up again, you can point to what was agreed.
explorer.agencyTitle: Ask a consumer agency for help
explorer.agencyBody: Consumer agencies exist for this moment. Share your messages and the replies. They can tell you which rules apply where you live.
explorer.agencyEUText: your national consumer authority or data-protection authority.

ask.title: Ask in writing
ask.lead: Send a short, polite note. Ask whether software helped make the decision, what information it used, and the main reasons.
ask.why: A written question gives you and the company the same clear record. It also gives their team a chance to spot a mistake early.
ask.sample: Hello. I received a decision about [my application] on [date]. Could you tell me whether an automated system helped make it, what information about me it used, and the main reasons? Thank you for your help.
ask.rule1: A lender that turns you down must give the specific main reasons, or tell you how to ask for them. (Regulation B)
ask.rule2: You can ask for your data and for meaningful information about how an automated decision was made. (GDPR, Article 15)

review.title: Request human review
review.lead: Ask for a person to look at your case. Add any facts the system may not have had.
review.why: A person can weigh details that software may miss, such as a recent change in your situation or an error in your records.
review.sample: Thank you for your reply. I would like a person to review this decision. Here is information that may help: [details]. Please let me know what else you need from me.
review.rule1: When a machine alone makes a decision with a legal or similarly serious effect on you, you can ask for a person to step in. (GDPR, Article 22)
review.rule2: The 2022 Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights recommends a way to reach a person. It is not law, and it has been archived.

dialogue.title: Keep the conversation constructive
dialogue.lead: If you still disagree, say what you think went wrong and what would fix it. Keep it specific and calm.
dialogue.why: Clear, specific feedback is easier to act on. It can help fix the process for the next person too.
dialogue.sample: Thank you for looking at this again. I still think [the specific issue]. A fair fix would be [what you are asking for]. Can we find a way forward together?
dialogue.rule1: Existing consumer-protection law applies to AI. The FTC has said there is no AI exemption. (FTC, 2024)
dialogue.rule2: Almost every country bans misleading business practices. Your consumer agency can tell you what applies to you.

br.label: Brazil:
br.text: try <consumidor>consumidor.gov.br</consumidor> first (free; it works only with companies that have joined). If that does not solve it, go to your local Procon (<procon>what Procon does</procon>). For personal data, ask the company first, then <anpd>petition the ANPD</anpd> (free, with a gov.br login; it uses petitions to plan its work and does not reply to each one).

fr.label: France:
fr.text: report a problem with a business on <signalconso>SignalConso</signalconso>. For your personal data or an automated decision, <cnil>complain to the CNIL</cnil>.

de.label: Germany:
de.text: for problems with AI, use the <bnetza>free AI complaint office of the Bundesnetzagentur</bnetza>. For personal data, contact your state data protection authority; <bfdi>the BfDI explains which one</bfdi>. For advice, sometimes for a fee, <vz>your Verbraucherzentrale</vz>.

in.label: India:
in.text: call the National Consumer Helpline on <tel>1915</tel> (free, 8 AM to 8 PM), or <nch>complain online</nch>. For AI-made content on a platform, complain to the platform's grievance officer first, then <gac>appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee</gac>.

it.label: Italy:
it.text: for personal data, <garante>complain to the Garante</garante> (free; ask the company first, and it must answer within a month). For an unfair business practice, <agcm>report it to the AGCM</agcm> (free; it can act against the practice but cannot get you a refund). AGCM phone line: <tel>800 166 661</tel>, weekdays 10:00 to 14:00.

Help.comingLead: These guides are still being written. <forum>Tell us in the forum</forum> what you need most.
Help.letterLead: Fill in the blanks, and the letter updates as you type. Send it by email, through the company's website, or by post. Keep a copy.
Help.companyHeading: If this letter reaches you at work
Help.companyLead: Thank you for reading it. Nobody is being blamed here. Most people who write just want to understand and be treated fairly. Here are some ideas that help.
Help.companyClose: A clear, kind answer can settle things for both sides. Working inside a company? <forum>Your view is welcome in the forum too</forum>.
Help.urgentHeading: When to get help from a person soon
Help.urgent: If you could lose your home, your job, or money you need for food or bills, don't wait for letters. A legal aid office or consumer advice centre near you can help. Many are free.
Help.record: Keep every letter, email, and notice, with its date. For phone calls, write down the date, who you spoke to, and what they said.
Help.forum: Should this work differently? <forum>Say what should change in the forum</forum>.

credit.metaTitle: A loan or credit was refused
credit.metaDescription: Your right to know why a loan or credit was refused, how to ask for a person to look again, and a letter you can send.
credit.title: A loan or credit was refused
credit.summary: A bank, card company, or lender said no, or offered worse terms.
credit.lead: A bank, card company, or other lender said no, or offered you worse terms. A score worked out by a computer often plays a part. You can ask why, and you can ask a person to look again.

happened.score: Lenders often use a credit score: a number a computer works out from your payment history and other data.
happened.automatic: Sometimes the whole decision is automatic. Sometimes a person decides, using the score.
happened.mistakes: Mistakes happen. Old or wrong data in your file can pull your score down.

company.answer: Reply soon, even just to say it arrived and when to expect a full answer. The deadlines above are the latest you can answer, not the goal.
company.reasons: Give the real main reasons, in plain words. “You didn't reach our score” leaves people guessing. The factors that counted most help them understand and improve. In the US, a score alone isn't enough as a reason.
company.person: Let a person look again, someone who can change the decision, not only repeat it.
company.data: Check the data. If something was wrong or out of date, fix it where it came from, and tell the person what changed.
company.patterns: Share what you learn. If similar letters keep coming, they may point to a step in the process worth improving.

rights.1: The lender must tell you why. The notice must give the main reasons. Saying only that you didn't reach their score is not enough.
rights.2: If they didn't give reasons, ask within 60 days. They must then give you the reasons within 30 days.
rights.3: If they used a credit report, they must name the credit bureau, and tell you that you can get a free copy of your report within 60 days and dispute anything wrong.
rights.4: The credit bureau must check a dispute for free, usually within 30 days.

us.noReply: If you get no answer within 30 days, send the letter again and mention the date of your first one. You can also <cfpb>file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau</cfpb>.

rights.1: You can ask for copies of your data. Organisations usually have one month to answer.
rights.2: If a computer alone made a significant decision about you, with no meaningful human involvement, the lender must let you get information about it, give your side, ask for a person to step in, and challenge it.
rights.3: These UK rules have applied since 5 February 2026. The UK left the EU, so its own version of the law applies.
rights.4: The Financial Ombudsman is free. Complain to the lender first. Most lenders have up to 8 weeks to sort it out. After their final answer, you have 6 months to go to the ombudsman.

uk.noReply: If you get no answer, or you disagree with it, you can take a lending complaint to the <fos>Financial Ombudsman Service</fos> for free. For how your data was used, you can complain to the <ico>Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)</ico>.

rights.1: You can ask for your data and how the decision was made. If it was automated, they must give you meaningful information about the logic involved, and what it meant for you.
rights.2: If a computer alone made the decision, you can usually ask for a person to review it, give your side, and challenge it.
rights.3: A credit score can count as the decision itself when a lender relies on it heavily. Then these rules apply to the company that made the score too.
rights.4: They must answer within one month, for free. For hard cases they can take two more months, but they must tell you within the first month.

eu.noReply: If you get no answer within one month, send a reminder. Then you can complain for free to the data protection authority in your country. <edpb>Find yours on the list of EU data protection authorities</edpb>.

rights.1: You can ask for a review of a decision made only by a computer, including decisions about your credit profile.
rights.2: You can ask for the criteria and steps used to reach the decision. Trade secrets can limit the details.
rights.3: You can see and correct your data. A clear, full statement of your data is due within 15 days of your request.
rights.4: The law doesn't say a person must do the review. That rule was removed in 2019, so ask for a person anyway.

br.noReply: If you get no answer, you can file a free petition with the <anpd>national data protection authority (ANPD)</anpd>, or a complaint on <consumidor>Consumidor.gov.br</consumidor> or with your local <procon>Procon</procon>.

rights.1: India's data protection law gives you the right to a summary of your data and to correct it, but these rights start in May 2027.
rights.2: You can still ask now. Write to the lender and ask for the reasons and for a person to look again. A written request gives you a record.

in.noReply: If you get no answer, the <nch>National Consumer Helpline</nch> can help. Call <tel>1915</tel>, toll-free.

rights.1: This site doesn't cover your country's laws yet. A written request is still worth sending: it asks clearly, and it gives you a record.

other.noReply: If you get no answer, look for a consumer protection or data protection authority in your country.

us.subject: Request for the reasons my credit application was refused{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
us.body:
Hello,

On {decisionDate}, you refused my application for credit. Under Regulation B (12 CFR 1002.9), I am asking for the specific reasons for this decision.

If you used a credit report or credit score, please tell me which credit bureau provided it and what score you used.

I would also like a person to look at my application again. If any of my information was wrong or out of date, I am ready to correct it.

Please reply in writing within 30 days.

Thank you,
{name}

uk.subject: Request under UK GDPR Articles 15 and 22C{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
uk.body:
Hello,

On {decisionDate}, you refused my application for credit. Under Article 15 of the UK GDPR, please send me a copy of the personal data you hold about me, tell me where it came from, and tell me whether the decision was made by automated means.

If the decision was based solely on automated processing, with no meaningful human involvement, I ask under Article 22C for information about it. I want to make representations, to have a person step in, and to contest the decision.

Please reply within one month.

Kind regards,
{name}

eu.subject: Request under GDPR Articles 15 and 22{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
eu.body:
Hello,

On {decisionDate}, you refused my application for credit. Under Article 15 of the GDPR, please send me:
- a copy of the personal data you hold about me, and where it came from;
- whether the decision was automated and, if so, meaningful information about the logic involved and what it means for me.

If the decision was based solely on automated processing, I ask under Article 22(3) for a person to review it. I want to give my point of view and to contest the decision.

Please reply within one month, as Article 12(3) requires.

Kind regards,
{name}

br.subject: Request under Articles 18, 19 and 20 of the LGPD{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
br.body:
Hello,

On {decisionDate}, you refused my application for credit. Under Articles 18 and 19 of the LGPD (Law No. 13,709/2018), please confirm whether you process my personal data, and send me a clear and complete statement of it, with its origin, the criteria used, and the purpose, within 15 days.

Under Article 20, I ask for a review of this decision, and for clear information on the criteria and procedures used to make it. I would like a person to carry out the review.

Kind regards,
{name}

plain.subject: Request for the reasons for a credit decision{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
plain.body:
Hello,

On {decisionDate}, you refused my application for credit. Please tell me the main reasons for this decision, and whether a computer system or score played a part.

Please also tell me what information about me you used, so I can check that it is correct. I would like a person to look at my application again.

I look forward to your reply in writing.

Kind regards,
{name}

job.metaTitle: A job application was screened out
job.metaDescription: What to do when software may have screened out your job application: your rights, a letter asking what happened, and where to turn.
job.title: A job application was screened out
job.summary: You applied for a job and heard nothing, or got a quick no.
job.lead: You applied for a job and heard nothing back, or got a fast rejection. Software may have sorted or scored your application. You can ask what happened, ask for a person to look, and ask for another way in if a test doesn't work for you.

happened.screening: Many employers use software to sort applications. It can scan CVs for keywords, or score online tests and video interviews.
happened.unread: An application the software ranks low may never be read by a person.
happened.mistakes: Tools can miss things: an unusual job title, a career break, or a layout the software can't read.

company.answer: Reply, even briefly. A short note that a decision was made is kinder than silence.
company.feedback: Share a little honest feedback. One or two points help people improve their next application.
company.person: Let a person look again when someone asks, especially if the software may have missed something.
company.access: Offer another way in. If a test or tool doesn't work for someone, for example because of a disability, an alternative keeps good candidates in the running. In the US, the law usually requires reasonable accommodations.
company.patterns: Check the tool now and then. If similar people keep getting screened out, its settings may need a look.

rights.1: If a background check was used and they plan to turn you down because of it, they must first give you a copy of the report and a summary of your rights.
rights.2: If you have a disability, you can ask for a reasonable accommodation, such as another way to take an online test. Tests must measure your skills, not your disability.
rights.3: In New York City, employers using automated hiring tools must have them checked for bias every year, publish information about it, and tell candidates 10 business days before using them.
rights.4: No federal law gives you a general right to know why you weren't hired. Asking politely can still help, and a written request gives you a record.

us.noReply: If a background check had wrong information, you can dispute it with the company that made it, and <cfpb>complain to the CFPB</cfpb>. If you think you were screened out because of disability, race, sex, age, or another protected trait, you can <eeoc>file a charge with the EEOC</eeoc>. The deadline is usually 180 days, or 300 in many states, so don't wait.

rights.1: You can ask for copies of your data, including notes and scores about your application. Organisations usually have one month to answer.
rights.2: If a computer alone turned you down, with no meaningful human involvement, and the decision significantly affects you, the employer must let you get information about it, give your side, ask for a person to step in, and challenge it.

uk.noReply: If you get no answer, or you disagree with it, you can complain to the <ico>Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)</ico> about how your data was used.

rights.1: You can ask for your data and how the decision was made, including scores and notes. If it was automated, they must give you meaningful information about the logic involved.
rights.2: Recruiting with no human involvement is one of the GDPR's own examples of a decision a computer shouldn't make alone. You can usually ask for a person to review it, give your side, and challenge it.
rights.3: New EU AI rules for hiring tools start on 2 December 2027. Until then, the data protection rights above apply.
rights.4: They must answer within one month, for free. For hard cases they can take two more months, but they must tell you within the first month.

eu.noReply: If you get no answer within one month, send a reminder. Then you can complain for free to the data protection authority in your country. <edpb>Find yours on the list of EU data protection authorities</edpb>.

rights.1: You can ask for a review of a decision made only by a computer, including decisions about your professional profile.
rights.2: You can ask for the criteria and steps used. Trade secrets can limit the details.
rights.3: You can see and correct your data. A clear, full statement of your data is due within 15 days of your request.
rights.4: The law doesn't say a person must do the review. That rule was removed in 2019, so ask for a person anyway.

br.noReply: If you get no answer, you can file a free petition with the <anpd>national data protection authority (ANPD)</anpd>.

rights.1: India's data protection law gives you the right to a summary of your data and to correct it, but these rights start in May 2027.
rights.2: You can still ask now. Write to the employer and ask whether software screened your application, and for a person to look again. A written request gives you a record.

in.noReply: If you get no answer, keep your letter and any replies. This site doesn't yet list a place in India to take hiring complaints.

rights.1: This site doesn't cover your country's laws yet. A written request is still worth sending: it asks clearly, and it gives you a record.

other.noReply: If you get no answer, look for a data protection authority or an equality body in your country.

us.subject: Question about my job application{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
us.body:
Hello,

On {decisionDate}, I learned that my application was not successful. I would be grateful for some feedback on the main reasons, and I would like to know whether an automated tool was used to screen or score my application.

If a background check or other consumer report played any part, please send me a copy of it and the summary of my rights that the Fair Credit Reporting Act provides for.

I would also appreciate it if a person could look at my application again.

Thank you for your time,
{name}

uk.subject: Request under UK GDPR Articles 15 and 22C about my job application{hasReference, select, yes { (ref. {reference})} other {}}
uk.body:
Hello,

- a copy of the personal data you hold about me, including any scores or notes about my application, and where it came from;

If the decision was based solely on automated processing, I ask under Article 22(3) for a person to review it. I want to give my point of view and to contest the decision.

Please reply within one month, as Article 12(3) requires.

Kind regards,

Hello,

Kind regards,

housing.metaTitle: A rental application was turned down
housing.metaDescription: What to do when a tenant screening check may have cost you a home: your rights, a letter asking what happened, and where to turn.
housing.title: A rental application was turned down
housing.summary: A landlord or letting agent said no, maybe after a screening check.
housing.lead: You applied to rent a home and the landlord or agent said no, or asked for a much bigger deposit. A screening check or score may have played a part. You can ask what was used, check it for mistakes, and ask for a person to look again.

happened.screening: Many landlords and letting agents use screening services. They can check credit, rental history, court records, and ID.
happened.score: Some services turn this into a score, or a simple yes or no.
happened.mistakes: Mistakes happen: an old record, a debt already paid, or a record that belongs to someone else.

company.answer: Reply, even briefly. People looking for a home are often under time pressure. A quick answer lets them move on or fix things.
company.reasons: Say what counted. If a screening report was used, say which company made it, so the person can check it. In the US, that is required.
company.person: Let a person look again, especially if the report might be about someone else.
company.data: If a record turns out to be wrong, tell the screening company and the applicant, so it doesn't happen again.
company.patterns: Check what your screening looks at. Old or unrelated records can shut out good tenants.

rights.1: Tenant screening reports count as consumer reports. If a landlord turns you down because of one, they must tell you which company supplied it, that the company didn't make the decision, and that you can get a free copy within 60 days and dispute anything wrong.
rights.2: The screening company must check a dispute for free, usually within 30 days.
rights.3: Housing discrimination is illegal because of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability.
rights.4: No federal law makes a landlord explain every reason for saying no. Asking politely can still help, and a written request gives you a record.

us.noReply: If a screening report had wrong information, dispute it with the company that made it, and <cfpb>complain to the CFPB</cfpb>. If you think you were turned down because of a protected trait, you can <hud>report it to HUD</hud> for free. The deadline is one year.

rights.1: You can ask for copies of your data, including any screening or credit check. Organisations usually have one month to answer.
rights.2: If a computer alone turned you down, with no meaningful human involvement, and the decision significantly affects you, they must let you get information about it, give your side, ask for a person to step in, and challenge it.

uk.noReply: If you get no answer, or you disagree with it, you can complain to the <ico>Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)</ico> about how your data was used.

rights.1: You can ask the landlord or agent for your data and how the decision was made. If it was automated, they must give you meaningful information about the logic involved.
rights.2: If a computer alone made the decision, you can usually ask for a person to review it, give your side, and challenge it.
rights.3: If they used a credit check or score from another company, you can ask that company too for the data it holds about you and where it came from.
rights.4: They must answer within one month, for free. For hard cases they can take two more months, but they must tell you within the first month.

eu.noReply: If you get no answer within one month, send a reminder. Then you can complain for free to the data protection authority in your country. <edpb>Find yours on the list of EU data protection authorities</edpb>.

rights.1: You can ask for a review of a decision made only by a computer, including decisions based on your consumer or credit profile.
rights.2: You can ask for the criteria and steps used. Trade secrets can limit the details.
rights.3: You can see and correct your data. A clear, full statement of your data is due within 15 days of your request.
rights.4: The law doesn't say a person must do the review. That rule was removed in 2019, so ask for a person anyway.

br.noReply: If you get no answer, you can file a free petition with the <anpd>national data protection authority (ANPD)</anpd>.

rights.1: India's data protection law gives you the right to a summary of your data and to correct it, but these rights start in May 2027.
rights.2: You can still ask now. Write to the landlord or agent, ask whether a screening check or score was used, and ask for a person to look again. A written request gives you a record.

in.noReply: If you get no answer, keep your letter and any replies. This site doesn't yet list a place in India to take rental screening complaints.

rights.1: This site doesn't cover your country's laws yet. A written request is still worth sending: it asks clearly, and it gives you a record.

other.noReply: If you get no answer, look for a data protection authority, a housing advice service, or an equality body in your country.

PAUSEStrategy.title: The PAUSE Strategy
PAUSEStrategy.subtitle: Your 5-Step Everyday AI Habit
PAUSEStrategy.tablistLabel: The five steps of the PAUSE Strategy
PAUSEStrategy.hint: Use the arrow keys or tap a letter to move between the steps.

protect.title: Protect Your Information
protect.body: Never paste account numbers, passwords, or confidential medical/financial details into public AI tools. Check your privacy settings to opt out of model training data collection where available.

assess.title: Assess Accuracy
assess.body: AI models predict pattern-based text—they don't 'know' facts. For critical health, financial, or legal decisions, always verify generated answers against primary human sources.

understand.title: Understand Purpose & Data
understand.body: Ask what information the tool relies on, whether it was independently tested, and if it carries hidden biases or commercial motivations.

seek.title: Seek Someone Accountable
seek.body: AI systems are human-led. Look for clear organizational contact channels and verify that a responsible human oversight team stands behind the technology.

exit.title: Exit & Escalate
exit.body: You always have the right to stop using a product, request data deletion, or report errors and unfair automated outcomes to consumer protection agencies.

Forum.metaDescription: Vote on short statements about AI and your rights, or suggest one. No account needed. Common ground is shown first.
Forum.title: Your voice belongs here
Forum.lead: Technology works best when everyone participates in shaping it. Vote on short statements, or suggest your own. No account needed.
Forum.civility: Your input is reviewed for civil discourse standards. We critique ideas, not people.
Forum.privacy: What we keep when you vote: your vote, the page language, and a random code saved in your browser so each person votes once. We don't store your name, email, or IP address with it. Votes are stored in a Neon database in Frankfurt, Germany. Like most websites, our host, Vercel, keeps short-term request logs that include IP addresses, for security. “Clear my votes” deletes them.

principles.heading: Follow five principles of constructive dialogue
principles.lead: These keep the forum useful for everyone. Each statement stands on its own, so there are no reply threads to argue in.
principles.critiqueText: Disagree with an idea as clearly as you like. Leave the person out of it.
principles.goodFaithText: Most people are doing their best with what they know. Ask before you assume harm.
principles.positivityText: Encouragement and rigor work together. Be kind and be specific.
principles.ethicsText: Say when AI helped you write something, cite your sources, and be honest about what you do not know.
principles.liftText: Share what you learn so the next person has an easier time.

vote.heading: Vote on {count} statements
vote.lead: Pick Agree, Disagree, or Pass for each one. The statements cover {tracks} tracks: {trackList}. Use Tab to reach the buttons and the arrow keys to move between them.

suggest.heading: Add a statement of your own

results.heading: See where people agree
results.lead: Results show common ground, not the loudest voices. Votes are grouped by the language people vote in. A statement counts as broad agreement only when every language group supports it.

loop.heading: Track what changes because of you
loop.lead: Every question leads to a visible outcome. This card is updated each time votes shape a guide or resource on this site.
loop.title: We asked, you said, we did
loop.saidText: No results yet. Areas of broad agreement will appear here once enough people vote.
loop.didText: Nothing yet. Each change will be listed here with its date and a link to the page it changed.

statements.t1-disclose: Automated assistants should say they are AI at the start of a conversation.
statements.t1-credentials: Photos, audio, and video made with AI should carry a label that shows how they were made.
statements.t2-reasons: When software helps make a decision about you, you should get the top reasons in plain language.
statements.t2-person: Every automated decision that affects you should come with a clear way to reach a person.
statements.t3-optin: Using your conversations to train AI should stay off unless you choose to turn it on.
statements.t3-clear: You should be able to clear your chat history with one tap.
statements.t4-together: People, educators, regulators, and companies should shape AI rules together.
statements.t4-accountable: Organizations should take responsibility for what their AI tools tell customers.

voting.disagreeTip: You do not support this statement.
voting.passTip: Skip it. You are unsure, or it does not apply to you.
voting.recordedAll: Recorded: {choice}. You have answered all {total} statements.
voting.doneTitle: Thank you. You answered every statement.
voting.clear: Clear my votes and start over
voting.unsent: {count, plural, one {1 vote has} other {# votes have}} not been sent yet. We will try again on your next vote or visit.
voting.clearFailed: We could not clear your votes. Check your connection and try again.

submission.label: Suggest a statement for others to vote on
submission.disclosure: A person reads every statement before it is shown. First, an AI model checks it for names and contact details: Mistral Small, or Google's Gemini as a backup, both on EU servers. It runs through OpenRouter, set not to keep your text. Approved statements are shown to people who use the same language. Statements that single out a person, company, or group are not published. Please leave out personal details. Your input is reviewed for civil discourse standards. We critique ideas, not people.
submission.placeholder: e.g., 'Customer service portals should always let you request a human representative with one tap.'
submission.sent: Thank you. Your statement is waiting for review.
submission.contact: Please remove links, email addresses, social media handles, and phone numbers, then try again.
submission.busy: The suggestion box is full for today. Please try again tomorrow. Your text is still in the box.
submission.failed: Your statement could not be sent. Check your connection and try again. Your text is still in the box.

consensus.heading: Where groups agree
consensus.lead: Common ground comes first. A statement shows here only when at least {minGroups} language groups each have {minVotes} or more votes on it, and every one of those groups agrees at {threshold}% or more. Passes are not counted.
consensus.noVotes: No votes have been counted yet.
consensus.progress: {votes, plural, one {1 vote counted so far, from {languages, plural, one {1 language} other {# languages}}.} other {# votes counted so far, from {languages, plural, one {1 language} other {# languages}}.}}
consensus.none: No statement has broad agreement yet.
consensus.summary: At least {percent}% agree in every language group:
consensus.error: Results could not be loaded right now. Please try again later.

About.metaDescription: Why this site exists, how it keeps dialogue fair and open, and who reviews its pages.
About.title: About this site
About.lead: This site explains your rights when AI makes decisions about you, in plain language and without blame. It compares approaches in the US and the EU, and it invites everyone into the conversation.
About.mission: Make AI consumer rights easy to understand, and easy to talk about. People who use AI, educators, regulators, and teams that build AI all have a stake. This site starts from the view that each of them is acting in good faith and doing their best with what they know. It critiques ideas and systems, never people.
About.safeguardsLead: These rules keep the site fair, open, and hard to misuse.

safeguards.trace: Every question leads somewhere you can see
safeguards.traceText: When forum votes change a guide or resource, the change is listed with its date. This is the "We asked, you said, we did" record.
safeguards.isolatedText: The forum has no reply threads. You vote on one short statement at a time, which leaves little room for spam or pile-ons.
safeguards.accessText: You do not need an account to vote. Pages aim for a grade 6 to 8 reading level and are built and tested against WCAG 2.2 Level AA.
safeguards.commonText: Results highlight what different groups agree on, not what divides them.
safeguards.sturdyText: The guide and other pages are plain static pages, kept separate from anything interactive, so they load quickly and keep working.

About.who: Robert Sweetman runs this site. AI models helped research and draft it. A person reviews every page before launch. The footer on each page lists which models helped, which sources back the facts, and where review stands.
About.whoLink: See every source and how it was checked
About.joinLead: Your view helps shape what comes next.
About.joinLink: Vote on shared ideas in the forum

Attribution.translationThanks: My grandparents, Giuffrido and Isolina DiCenso, left Italy for a new country and learned a new language. Their journey inspired these translations. With love and thanks to them and to my parents, Joanne Sweetman and Robert Sweetman Sr.
Attribution.registryAbout: Every source this site draws on, with how each link was checked. “Link opened by AI and matched” means an AI model (Claude, or research agents it directed) opened the link on the checked date and the content matched what this site says. That is not the same as a person reading it. Robert is reading every source himself; each one he has read says so, with the date. “Link not yet opened” means the link comes from an official index or search, but no one has opened it yet. “No public link yet” means it is listed as background reading, with no public link recorded. Every link also has a copy saved at the Internet Archive, so anyone can see the page as it was when it was checked. Sources Robert has read show the fingerprint of his own copy, so anyone with the same file can confirm it matches.

HowItWorks.metaDescription: Every service this site uses, what each one sees, what we keep, and what isn't finished.
HowItWorks.title: How this site works
HowItWorks.lead: This site asks companies to explain their AI in plain words. So here is how this site works, in plain words, including what isn't finished.
HowItWorks.who: Robert Sweetman, on his own. No money, sponsors, or investors are behind it. No ads, no tracking, no analytics.
HowItWorks.open: Open by design. The code is public on GitHub under the MIT license. The writing is free to reuse with credit, under CC BY 4.0.
HowItWorks.mission: <mission>Read the mission and values this site holds itself to</mission>.
HowItWorks.built: Robert built it with AI help. Claude wrote most of the code with him, and several AI models helped research and draft the guide; the footer on each page names them. A person is still reviewing every page.
HowItWorks.servicesHeading: Services we use, and what each one sees

services.vercel: Vercel hosts the site and its firewall. It sees each visit, including IP addresses, in short-term logs.
services.neon: Neon is the database, in Frankfurt, Germany. It holds votes, stored with a scrambled browser code, and suggested statements.
services.openrouter: OpenRouter passes each suggested statement to an AI model. It keeps usage records (time, model, cost) but not your text, and it only uses services that don't keep it either.
services.models: Mistral Small, with Google's Gemini as a backup, reads each suggestion on EU servers to flag names and contact details. It only flags; a person decides.
services.github: GitHub stores the public code. Proton handles email.

HowItWorks.keepHeading: What we keep, and for how long

keep.votes: Votes: until you press “Clear my votes.” The browser code lasts {days} days. We haven't set an automatic deletion date yet.
keep.suggestions: Suggestions: rejected ones are deleted. Approved ones stay while they're shown.
keep.letters: Letters: what you type into a letter stays on your device. It isn't sent to this site or saved.
keep.never: Never kept with your vote: your name, email, or IP address.

unfinished.review: Human review of the guide is still in progress.
unfinished.legal: The help pages and letters haven't been reviewed by a lawyer, legal clinic, or consumer organisation yet. We plan to ask for that review, and to name reviewers only with their permission.
unfinished.translations: The translations were made with AI help. Native speakers haven't checked all of them yet.
unfinished.language: Suggestions only appear in the language they were written in.
unfinished.results: Results appear only after {minVotes} or more votes per language, so early on there are none.
unfinished.ai: The AI check can be wrong. A person makes every decision.
unfinished.limits: To keep costs low, the AI checks at most {checks} suggestions a day. After that, a person still reads each one, without the AI check. After {max} suggestions in a day, the suggestion box pauses until the next day.
unfinished.twice: Voting without accounts can't fully stop someone from voting twice, for example by using a second browser.

HowItWorks.correctionsLead: When something on this site is wrong, we fix it and list it here, newest first. Each entry says what was wrong and what changed. We name the person who flagged it only if they ask.
HowItWorks.contact: Criticism is welcome when it comes with a reason. Tell us what's wrong, why it matters, and, if you can, how to fix it.
HowItWorks.contactHow: Email <mail>{email}</mail>, or <issues>open an issue on GitHub</issues>.
HowItWorks.reviewers: Can you review the help pages or letters? Lawyers, legal clinics, consumer organisations, and native speakers are all welcome. Write to {email}. We name reviewers only with their permission, and a no needs no explanation.
